title: Chapter 217 – Four Breaths a Minute
html:
[Terrace Five – Jian]

The first thing the sitting takes is his sense of time.

It does not take it dramatically. There is no wrench, no dizzy lurch of the stomach. He bites the amber fruit and swallows, and the taste is warm and faintly sour, like a plum left on the sill in sunlight, and then the world simply loosens. The tick of the Orchard slows. The golden light thickens. He is aware of a hand on his shoulder, Veyra's, light as a leaf, and then he is not aware of it, because the hand has become a very long time ago.

He sits.

For a while he does what he has been trained to do. He draws breath, and sinks it to the lower field below the navel, and lets the old circuit of the Core turn. The qi is thick here. It comes up from the white stone of the bench and down from the brass leaves of the tree, and it tastes of resin and honey. The Core spins, a heavy bright wheel, and he feels the cracks in it where the Print mended and the tremor in his meridians where the mending ended. Eighty-two percent. He notes it, as a clerk notes a figure.

```
ARK-7 // SITTING LEDGER
Location: Terrace Five, Ripening Row 5, Tree 17.
Rate of passage: 1 Orchard day = 40 outside days.
Fare: 1 year of lifespan per Orchard year.
Lifespan: 91y 213d
Core: 82%. Print: LOCKED (Ring severed). Scan: ONLINE.
Projected Nascent Soul seed: 1 Orchard year, +/- 90 days.
```

He reads it once, carefully, and lets it go.

This is the cost, he thinks. This is what the Orchard has been waiting for me to say. Yes. Yes to the arithmetic. Yes to the ledger. Yes to the idea that a year of my life is a fair price for eighty of theirs.

The circuit turns. The bench is warm. The tree ticks, very slow, very far, like a clock in the next house.

He lets himself go down into the work.

---

It is not easy, and it is not pleasant, and it is not what the books describe.

The books say that the Nascent Soul is born of the Core, as a chick from an egg. They speak of a golden moment, a flowering of the dantian, a soul-child who sits in the lotus and smiles. They are written by men who have never done it, or by men who have done it and been sworn to silence.

What happens is a drowning.

He feels it start in the third week, by the Orchard's count. The Core begins to compress. Slowly, then more quickly, it shrinks inward on itself, like a star on the edge of becoming something else, and the qi that fed it comes back in a tide that is almost too thick to breathe. His meridians burn. His left hand, the one the tremor has taken, goes numb to the wrist, then to the elbow, and he finds himself watching it as a man watches a river he has no way to cross. He cannot move it. He cannot feel it. He thinks, quite calmly: this is the cost.

The tree above him ticks twice.

Veyra Thann, who is somewhere very far away, says something he does not catch. He thinks it is a name. He thinks it is Orrin, or perhaps Sera. The word falls through the dark like a coin down a well.

Hold, he tells himself.

He holds.

---

On the fortieth Orchard day, the compression stops.

It does not end. It simply reaches the limit of what the Core can compress, and the pressure turns around like a held breath released. He feels the Core go dark. It is a small, clean, absolute darkness, and for the length of a long pulse he is nothing: not a man, not a name, not a pair of hands. A point of attention, tuned to a single question.

What am I for?

It is not his question. It is the tree's.

He knows that at once, in the dark, with the cold clarity that comes at the bottom of any deep thing. The Orchard asks it of everyone who sits. It asks it so that the answer can be grown. A man who sits under a tree with no purpose grows nothing. A man who sits with a purpose that is not his own grows something terrible. The Founders knew that. They built the Terraces to ask it.

He thinks of the answer he would have given a year ago.

To survive.

He thinks of the answer he would have given in the Hall of Ten Thousand Names, at the moment of the Mending, with nine friends giving a day apiece to mend a stranger's core.

To make it worth what they paid.

He thinks of Mo Yan's small hands on the Ferryman's black glass bell, and of Hua in the dust with her mark on fire, and of Wenyuan, alone in a tower, writing the tower is very kind to me.

To not be the thing that costs them, he thinks.

The darkness gives a faint, soft tick.

It is not the right answer. He knows it before the tree does. It is a good answer, a true answer, a human one, and it is not the answer the Orchard is asking for. The Orchard is asking a different question. It is asking: what will you do with the years?

And he does not know.

---

The dream begins as a smell: cut grass, and tallow, and a thin sharp edge of metal.

He is standing in a long stone room with a great round window at the far end. The window looks out on a sky he has not seen before, a sky the color of a bruise, torn across the middle by a seam of pale fire. It is the Seam, but newer: cleaner, narrower, a bright crack in the dark. Around him, in a ring, nine empty chairs stand on a dais of white stone.

Not chairs. He sees that as he steps closer. They are seats, deep and narrow, carved from a single block, each with a runnel for the feet and a rest for the hands. In the center of each is a small round socket, the size of a plum.

They are sockets for hours, says a voice.

It is the voice of a man.

Jian turns. A tall, awkward, bearded man is sitting at the end of the dais with his sleeves rolled to the elbow and a pen behind his ear. He is perhaps thirty-five years old, and there is soil on his cheek, and his eyes, red-rimmed and bright, are fixed on the window with an expression of unbearable patience. Jian has not seen him before. He has seen him a hundred times.

Orrin, he says.

Yes. The man does not look up. I thought you would come eventually. They always come eventually. It is very lonely, being the only one who remembers the plan.

This is a memory.

It is a tree's memory of a man's memory. A faint smile. Rather like a letter read aloud by a child. It will be a little wrong. Forgive it.

Jian sits on the edge of the dais.

Tell me the plan, he says.

---

There were nine of us, says Orrin Thann.

Nine Founders. Nine voices. We came from a place that had been destroyed, a first world, a bright one, and we found the Seam in the new world before it had grown teeth. We thought we could mend it. The man's fingers move on his knee. We could not. But we could hold it. A Seam is a place where the world is thin. To hold it, you must keep one thing steady on the thin side and one on the thick. A voice, and a vow.

Nine voices.

One for each Terrace. Nine seats, nine sockets, nine hours burning at once. It was a good design. The bearded face softens. Do you know why nine? It is not magic. It is only that no one of us could bear the weight alone. It takes a single voice about six years to burn out. Nine voices, in rotation, can hold it for fifty-four. We thought we would find the way to mend it in that time.

You did not.

We did not. Orrin looks at the empty seats. Four of the Founders died in the first decade. One went mad. Two fled. One was Veyra. He is silent for a moment. I was the ninth. I was supposed to be the last, the one who closed the Door. And then the rest were gone, and the Seam did not care that there were fewer of us. It came on at the same speed.

So you held it alone.

I held it with hours. The man's laugh is dry. We had found the Orchard. We had found that a tree could take a year of life and make it into a coin, a very small bright coin, and that a coin could be burned in a socket. Not as good as a voice. But a voice can be borrowed. He turns his face, at last, to Jian. His eyes are the color of old river water. The passengers on the Road have been paying for six hundred years to keep the lamp lit. They did not know. I told them it was a fare. That is the nearest thing to a lie I ever told.

It was a lie.

It was a mercy. A lie that keeps the world is a mercy. Orrin's voice is very quiet. I know what you think of me. I know what Veyra thinks. I do not defend it. I only say that I did it for as long as I could.

Jian lowers his head.

And the Interface? he says.

Orrin is silent.

The thing in my head, Jian says. The panels. The Ring. It said it was built for nine hosts.

It was. The man's gaze goes to the window. It was the first thing we built, in the first world, before the end. A machine for sharing a burden among nine bodies. A design for a ring of nine, bound by a single mind, so that no one of them would have to burn alone. His mouth twists. It was meant to be used here. At this Door. It was lost on the journey. I do not know how it came to you. But I know what it was for.

To hold the Seam.

To hold it for ever, says Orrin. Without anyone dying.

The dream tilts.

Jian feels it in his stomach. He sees, all at once, with a cold, flat, devastating clarity, the shape of what he has been climbing toward. Not a god. Not a throne. A chair, in a circle of nine, at the top of a tower. A burden meant to be shared. A machine built to make it bearable.

He sees the Ring cut loose from his mind, a thread snapped by the eight who loved him too much to drag him down.

It is gone, he says. His voice cracks. The Ring is gone. They cut it. I cannot—

It can be rebuilt. Orrin leans forward, and for the first time his face is alive, urgent, young. That is the thing I want you to understand. A ring can be rebuilt. It requires only nine who are willing, and a mind to bind them. You have the mind. You have more than eight willing. You have, God help you, a great many. A shaky laugh. I did not have one.

Why did you not tell us?

I tried. The light in the window changes. I sent the key. I sent the map. I sent the shadow, in the end, because it was the only thing that could climb. But I did not send it. Something else did. He rises. The nine seats are fading, one by one, into the dark. It is listening, Lin Jian. It has been listening since the day I sealed the Door. And it has learned to use my hand.

The Bloom.

Be careful of what it offers, says Orrin Thann, as the dream thins. It will always offer you exactly what you want.

---

He wakes into pain.

It is the first real thing he has felt in a long time. A bright, wet, intimate pain, in the left hand, in the shoulder, in the whole of the left side of his body, as though he had been struck by lightning and then sewn up. He lets out a breath. It is a ragged one, and it hurts, and he is more grateful for it than he has ever been for anything.

He opens his eyes.

The Orchard is gold. The tree above him ticks, very slowly. Beside him, on the neighboring bench, Hua sits with her eyes closed and a faint dew of sweat on her brow, and her mark is glowing steadily through the cloth of her sleeve. A little farther away, on a stool, an old woman with a basket is dozing. Veyra Thann is standing at the gate with her back to him, a gray column in the honey light.

"How long?" he says.

His voice is a croak. Veyra does not turn.

Four hundred and eleven days, she says. By the Orchard.

Outside?

Forty-five years. A pause. You were quiet for a long time. I had begun to think—

She does not finish. Instead she turns her hooded head, very slightly, toward the far end of the Row, and he follows the movement and sees what he missed in the gold light: two more benches, under two more trees, and on each bench a sleeper. One is a boy with a shaven head. The other is a lean woman with a dark braid, sitting perfectly upright with her hands on her knees and her eyes closed.

They came up the stair forty Orchard days after you sat, says Veyra. The woman said you were expected. She would not be turned back. I did not try.

He knows the braid. He knows the set of the shoulders, the line of the jaw, the particular unyielding stillness. His chest tightens until it hurts.

Yue, he thinks.

The seed in his palm gives a single hard beat.

He tries to sit up, and finds that he can. The bench is under him. His hand, the left, which has been numb for a year, is warm and heavy and works. He lifts it, slowly, and turns it over in the golden light, and sees, with a small shock, that it does not shake.

The tremor is gone.

He stares at the hand. It is a plain, scarred, workman's hand, with a faint pale web along the knuckles where the Print once repaired it. It is entirely steady. He closes the fingers into a fist and opens them again, and a tiny gold light gathers in the palm, a small round point, like a seed.

Ah, says Veyra Thann, softly. There it is.

The panel appears.

```
ARK-7 // MILESTONE
Nascent Soul SEED formed. Stage: 0 (embryonic).
Core: converted. Lifespan: 90y 213d. (1 year consumed.)
Tremor (Print scar): RESOLVED. The tree mended what it broke.

NEW CAPABILITY: SCAN (Soul band).
Scan now resolves HOURS: you can read the fruit.
Cost: each reading burns one hour from the reader.
Scan can no longer be used without cost.

PRINT: still LOCKED. Reason: no Ring.
Known path to unlock: rebuild a Ring of nine hosts.
Known location: the Tenth Door.
```

He reads the whole of it. He reads it again.

The seed in his palm pulses, once, in time with his heart.

---

Veyra comes to him when Hua has gone back under.

He has asked her to. He sits on the white bench with his hands in his lap and the seed dim in his palm, and the Orchard ticks around them like a sleeping house, and when she crosses the grass he finds that he does not know how to begin. She stands in front of him. She has put back her hood.

You spoke in the sitting, she says.

"What did I say?"

Names. The river-colored eyes are steady. Orrin. Sera. Others I did not know. And a number.

"What number?"

Nine.

He looks at his hands.

He has a rule, an old one, older than the Interface: the machine is his alone, and what he does with its knowledge must look like his own judgment. He has kept it for three lives. He keeps it now. But he has also, in the dark of the sitting, been told something the machine did not tell him, by a man who had no reason to lie, and he finds that the rule has a gap in it exactly the shape of a husband.

"He told me about the Door," Jian says. "In a dream. In the tree. He said there were nine Founders. Nine voices, nine seats, one for each Terrace, to hold the Seam in rotation. Four died. One went mad. Two fled. One was you. And the ninth was him."

Veyra does not move.

"He said the Door was built for nine," Jian says. "And that when the rest were gone, he held it alone, with hours."

For a long time she says nothing.

He did not tell me that, she says at last.

"No."

He told me he had volunteered. The cool voice does not shake. He told me nobody else would. He said it was a choice he made. That he had decided that a husband who loved his wife would sooner stand at the Door than see her stand there. A silence. I believed him. I believed him for six hundred years.

"It was true."

It was true. It was also incomplete. Her ruined hand curls at her side. There were others. Of course there were others. I was one. I was a voice, and he made me a lock, and he put me to sleep so that I would not have to be the next to burn. Her mouth twists. That is the Founders' great gift, Lin Jian. They find the one thing you cannot say no to, and they ask for it in the name of something larger.

"I am sorry."

Do not be. She lifts her head. I have been carrying the wrong grief. I thought I was the woman who abandoned her husband. It seems I am the woman whose husband abandoned her. She almost laughs. It is a great deal easier to carry.

"He sent the key to wake you."

He did not. The voice sharpens. You said it yourself. The Bloom used his hand. She stands very still. I should like to think that he would have. I should like to think that he would have asked, if he could.

"I think he would."

Do you?

"I think—" Jian stops. He has seen a man in a dream, with soil on his cheek and eyes the color of old river water, say it is very lonely, being the only one who remembers the plan. "I think he was lonelier than any of us. And I think he made a very large number of mistakes. And I think he would give anything to be asked."

Veyra turns away.

She stands for a long time with her back to him and her gray cloak falling straight from her shoulders. The Orchard ticks. The light moves, very slowly, from honey to gold.

Then I shall ask him, she says. When I reach the Door.

---

The old woman wakes at the sixth Orchard hour, and finds him standing beside the nearest tree.

He has risen without asking leave. He is not strong; his knees shake and his breath comes short. But he has a thing to do, and the seed in his palm, small as a lentil, burning as a coal, will not let him put it off. He reaches up and takes a single amber fruit from the lowest bough.

"Careful," says Sorrel, behind him.

"I know."

"It will cost you."

"One hour." He turns the fruit in his fingers. "The Scan said so."

"One hour for every reading. And the fruit you choose will not be one you want." She rises, creaking, and her wrinkled face is grave. "Everyone wants to see the people they left. It is the first thing they ask. And it is the only thing I have ever begged them not to do."

"Why?"

"Because it is never what you hoped."

He looks at the fruit. Inside it, a small bright figure is walking across a small bright courtyard. It is a woman, he thinks, in a gray robe, with a streak of white in her dark hair.

"I know," he says. "I have to."

He closes his hand around the fruit and lets the Scan open.

It does not hurt. There is a click, soft and bright, like the turning of a key, and the Orchard slips sideways. The figure grows. The courtyard grows. He sees stone, and sky, and a cold gray morning, and the high pale shape of the Hall of Ten Thousand Names. He sees a woman in her sixties crossing a flagged yard with a stick in one hand and a bundle of scrolls in the other. Her hair is entirely white. Her back is straight. She stops at the foot of a flight of steps, and a young man in the gray tunic of the Hall's guard hurries down to take her bundle, and she smiles at him, and the smile is one he has seen a thousand times.

Mei, he thinks.

He watches her climb the steps. He watches her pause at the door. He watches her look back, over her shoulder, at something he cannot see, and her face goes quiet and tender and a little sad.

Then the hour burns out.

The fruit in his hand is dark, a dry husk, crumbling to dust. A faint ache settles behind his eyes. He sets his jaw against it.

"Sixty-four," he says. His voice is rough. "She looks about sixty-four."

"Then you have lost less than most," says Sorrel gently.

"She is alive."

"Yes."

"They are alive." He lets the dust fall through his fingers. "I thought I had made my peace with that. I had not."

The old woman puts a dry hand on his arm.

"You have another year in the tree," she says. "And a girl at your side who wakes tomorrow. And a long stair above that, with a door at the end of it." She smiles, and it splits her face. "I should rest, if I were you. Eat something. The Orchard is unkind, but it is not wasteful."

He nods. He turns, slowly, toward the bench, where Hua is stirring on her stool and the mark in her palm is burning a steady gold.

"Hua," he says.

She opens her eyes.

She comes up slowly, the way a swimmer comes up from deep water, and for a moment her eyes do not focus. The mark in her palm is a steady gold, like a coin held to a lamp. Her lips are cracked. There is a thin line of dried sweat along her hairline, and a new silver thread at her temple that was not there when she bit the fruit.

"How long?" she says.

"Forty-five years. Outside."

"And in here?"

"A year, and some days."

She closes her eyes again. He thinks she may have slept. Then she says, in a very small voice: "Did you see them?"

"One."

"Who?"

"Mei." He sits down beside her, carefully, and lets his shoulder rest against the trunk of the tree. "She is sixty-four. She uses a stick. She has white hair, and she smiles at the guards."

Hua is quiet for a long time.

"I saw the tower," she says. "In the sitting. I saw it in the dark, with the lamp burning. And a man in the window, with his back to me." She swallows. "He didn't turn around. I called, and he didn't turn around."

"Wenyuan."

"I don't know. It might have been anyone." She opens her eyes, and they are wet. "It might have been me."

He does not know what to say. He puts his steady hand over hers, the one with the mark, and the gold light spills between their fingers, and the Orchard ticks on around them, slow and golden, a thousand thousand years of other people's hours.

"We have another year," he says.

"I know."

"I would like to spend it well."

"So would I," says Hua. And then, with a ghost of her old dry humor: "Do you think there's tea?"
